paper_title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Unifying multimodal understanding and generation within single model has received growing attention in multimodal learning (OpenAI, 2024; Team, 2024; Chen et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024). Such unification offers the potential for visual generation to leverage knowledge acquired through multimodal understanding (OpenAI, 2024). However, jointly optimizing for understanding and generation remains challenging, as the two objectives can interfere with each other, potentially compromising understanding performance (Hao et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a). To mitigate such interference, recent unified multimodal models (UMMs) introduce generation-specific capacity to create 1 Figure 2 Qualitative examples of generation and editing. Prompts are abbreviated; bold text marks the part requiring diverse world knowledge, with its meaning in parentheses. Examples include WISE (Niu et al., 2026) and KRIS-Bench (Wu et al., 2025d) prompts. separate pathway for visual generation (Pan et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025). Such specialization poses challenge for the generation pathway to effectively leverage knowledge encoded in the understanding pathway. Prior work has explored architectural designs that connect pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to generative pathways through learnable queries (Pan et al., 2025), feature conditioning (Wu et al., 2026), or shared attention (Wang et al., 2026c; Shen et al., 2026). While these approaches allow generative pathways to access pretrained VLM representations, they typically model generation in separate, heterogeneous visual representation space, often defined by reconstruction-oriented VAEs (Esser et al., 2024; Labs, 2024; Wu et al., 2025a). Recent studies have highlighted the role of sharing visual representations in leveraging pretrained multimodal knowledge for generation (Wu et al., 2025b; Kang et al., 2026). However, directly using VLM representations for generation remains challenging, as their highlevel features often lack the fine-grained information required for image reconstruction (Chen et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025a). Adapting the vision encoder for reconstruction, in turn, can degrade its pretrained semantic capabilities (Wu et al., 2025c; Lin et al., 2025c; Yue et al., 2026). This raises the question of whether rich representations learned by pretrained VLMs for multimodal understanding can also be leveraged for visual generation without compromising their understanding capabilities. In this work, we propose Integral, unified multimodal modeling approach that extends pretrained vision-language model with visual generation in shared visual representation space while preserving its understanding capabilities. Our analysis suggests that key bottleneck in adapting pretrained vision encoders for reconstruction while preserving their semantic quality may lie in the retention of low-level features in deeper layers, potentially interfering with 2 (a) Joint vs. AF (Ours) (b) Layer-wise similarity (c) Semantics and reconstruction during training Figure 3 Propagation bottleneck and Abstraction Fusion (AF). (a) Joint training of the encoder requires low-level visual information to propagate to the final layer, whereas AF directly fuses features across the frozen encoder hierarchy. (b) Layer-wise CKA analysis shows that joint training increases the similarity between deeper layers and the initial-layer. (c) Joint training exhibits trade-off between semantic preservation and reconstruction fidelity during training, whereas AF largely avoids this trade-off. progressive semantic abstraction (Sec. 2.1). Based on this observation, we introduce Abstraction Fusion (AF), which aggregates representations across multiple abstraction levels of the frozen vision encoder into shared visual tokens for understanding and generation without altering the pretrained hierarchy. To efficiently leverage the understanding pathway for generation in this token space, we further introduce Block-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (Block-wise MoT), lightweight generative architecture that conditions on the VLMs internal representations at block boundaries. Contributions. We introduce Integral, which extends pretrained vision-language model with strong visual generation using only 0.89B generation-specific parameters while preserving its understanding capability. Integral achieves strong performance across compositional generation, knowledge-intensive generation, and image editing that requires multimodal understanding. Controlled comparisons show that sharing the visual representation space improves generative learning beyond what can be explained by reconstruction quality alone.

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: We introduce Integral, unified multimodal modeling approach that extends pretrained vision-language model with visual generation through shared visual token space while preserving its understanding capabilities. Integral consists of two key components. Abstraction Fusion (AF) constructs visual tokens that are used for both multimodal understanding and high-fidelity image reconstruction (Sec. 2.2). Block-wise MoT is lightweight generative architecture that learns conditional velocity field over using VLM representations at block boundaries (Sec. 2.3).

sections.title: 2.1 Propagation Bottleneck
sections.content: Our goal is to extend the representations learned by pretrained vision encoder to support image reconstruction while preserving their semantic quality, serving as shared space in both understanding and generation. key challenge is that representations become increasingly abstract across encoder depth, making fine-grained visual details difficult to recover from the final representation (Mahendran and Vedaldi, 2015; Li et al., 2024c). Adapting the vision encoder for reconstruction improves reconstruction fidelity but can degrade semantic quality, reflecting the semantics reconstruction trade-off shown in Fig. 3c and observed in prior unified representation learning (Wu et al., 2025c; Ma et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026). Prior work has primarily attributed the semanticsreconstruction trade-off to optimization difficulties or limited representation capacity (Ma et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2025). We investigate complementary explanation based on how information is transformed across the depth of the vision encoder. Vision encoders progressively transform local visual information into more abstract semantic representations (Yosinski et al., 2014; Mahendran and Vedaldi, 2015), while intermediate layers retain fine-grained visual details that are increasingly attenuated in deeper representations (Li et al., 2024c; Zhang et al., 2024). When reconstruction relies only on the final representation, training may encourage deeper layers to preserve information characteristic of earlier representations, potentially limiting progressive semantic abstraction (Fig. 3a). We refer to this hypothesis as propagation bottleneck. To examine this hypothesis, we analyze how joint training alters the representation hierarchy of the vision encoder. As shown in Fig. 3b, joint training of the vision encoder substantially increases this similarity in deeper layers relative to the pretrained encoder. Increasing semantic supervision reduces this similarity, consistent with greater representational differentiation across depth. Fig. 3c shows trade-off between semantic preservation and reconstruction fidelity during training, with stronger semantic supervision degrading reconstruction fidelity. Together, these results are consistent with our propagation bottleneck hypothesis. These observations suggest avoiding exclusive reliance on the final encoder representation for reconstruction. This motivates us to propose Abstraction Fusion (AF), which constructs visual tokens by aggregating representations across multiple abstraction levels of the frozen vision encoder without altering its encoder hierarchy (Fig. 3a). AF substantially improves reconstruction fidelity while maintaining semantics close to those of the frozen encoder (Fig. 3c).

Let denote the multimodal conditioning input including text and images, processed by the pretrained VLM with parameters θ. To predict the velocity field for noisy visual latents zt conditioned on the VLM representations of c, we employ Block-wise MoT, parameter-efficient variant of Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT; Liang et al. 2025). Block-wise MoT. Conventional MoT couples each VLM layer with generation-specific expert, enabling fine-grained interaction throughout the transformer hierarchy but introducing substantial parameter overhead (Fig. 5a). sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate the effectiveness of Integral as unified multimodal modeling approach that leverages pretrained VLM knowledge for visual generation. First, we show that Integral achieves strong multimodal understanding, text-toimage generation and image editing performance with only 0.89B generation-specific parameters (Sec. 3.2). Moreover, Integral achieves strong performance on knowledge-intensive generation tasks, suggesting that pretrained multimodal knowledge can be effectively leveraged for visual generation (Sec. 3.3). We further provide controlled comparisons to show that representation sharing enables visual generation to leverage pretrained multimodal knowledge (Sec. 3.4).

sections.title: 3.1 Setup
sections.content: We instantiate Integral with Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026), keeping the pretrained VLM frozen throughout training. Training consists of two phases: visual tokenizer training and conditional visual generation training. For visual tokenization, we first train AF at 256 256 resolution, followed by dynamic-resolution training up to 512 512. We then fine-tune the pixel decoder with adversarial supervision to improve perceptual reconstruction quality while keeping the learned visual token space fixed. For visual generation, we train Block-wise MoT on the learned AF visual tokens in three stages. We begin with text-to-image pretraining at 256256 resolution, followed by higher-resolution interleaved pretraining to support image-conditioned generation. Finally, we perform supervised fine-tuning on diverse generation tasks, including text-to-image generation, image editing, multi-reference generation, and interleaved reasoning. Full training details, including datasets and hyperparameters, are provided in Appendix A.2.

These results highlight the advantage of building upon pretrained VLMs, with Integral retaining 99.8% of the pretrained models understanding performance. Text-to-image generation. Building upon these strong understanding capabilities, Integral achieves competitive textto-image generation performance with only 0.89B generation-specific parameters. As shown in Tab. 3, Integral achieves GenEval score of 0.88, outperforming larger UMMs such as BAGEL (0.82) and TUNA-2 (0.87). In contrast, Integral combines shared visual representations with lightweight Block-wise MoT, sharing most of its model capacity across understanding and generation. We further investigate the generative benefits of representation sharing in Sec. 3.4. Image editing. sections.title: 3.4 Analysis of Representation Sharing
sections.content: To investigate the role of representation sharing in leveraging pretrained multimodal knowledge for visual generation, we compare AF with alternative visual tokenizers under controlled settings. Following our text-to-image pretraining setup, we train each variant for 50K steps with matched generative architectures and training settings. Shared visual representations improve generative learning. We first compare AF with FLUX.1-VAE (Labs, 2024), reconstruction-oriented VAE adopted in BAGEL (Deng et al., 2025) as generative latent. As shown in Figs. 1 and 6a, AF substantially improves generative learning over FLUX.1-VAE, achieving GenEval score of 0.41 compared with 0.18 under the same training steps (50K). Given their comparable reconstruction quality (32.2 vs. 31.1 dB PSNR), this gap suggests that sharing visual representations with the pretrained VLM benefits generative learning beyond reconstruction fidelity alone. VLM-native alignment improves generation beyond semantic alignment alone. To examine whether the generative benefits of AF arise simply from semantic representations, we compare AF with SigLIP2-AF, which applies the same AF architecture to an external semantic encoder (Tschannen et al., 2025). As shown in Fig. 6a, AF outperforms SigLIP2-AF (0.41 vs. 0.31 on GenEval), suggesting that sharing visual representations with the conditioning VLM provides additional generative benefits beyond benefits of semantic space. Shared representations better leverage pretrained VLM conditioning. To further examine whether representation sharing facilitates the use of pretrained multimodal knowledge, we compare VLM and text-only LLM conditioning for AF and FLUX.1-VAE. As shown in Fig. 6b, AF gains substantially more from VLM conditioning than FLUX.1-VAE (+0.13 vs. +0.01 on GenEval). Taken together, our results highlight the importance of sharing visual representations with the pretrained VLM to effectively leverage its multimodal knowledge for generation.

sections.title: 3.5 Scalability of Integral
sections.content: To examine the scalability of Integral, we extend our approach to the smaller Qwen3.5-2B backbone. With this 2B backbone, AF provides reconstruction PSNR of 32.33 dB while retaining 99.2% of the pretrained VLMs understanding performance (Tab. 8). For visual generation, Integral achieves GenEval score of 0.26 after 50K training steps, outperforming the 9B baseline using FLUX.1-VAE (0.18) under the same training budget. sections.title: 3.6 Component Analysis
sections.content: We further evaluate the effectiveness of the two key components of Integral, AF and Block-wise MoT, through comparisons with alternative architectures. Abstraction Fusion. To evaluate the effectiveness of AFs hierarchical feature fusion, we compare it with multi-layer summation (MLS; Singh et al. 2026) and attention pooling under 20K-step tokenizer training. As shown in Fig. 8, AF substantially improves reconstruction (+6.27 dB PSNR over MLS) while maintaining semantic similarity to the frozen baseline. In contrast, simpler aggregation methods exhibit trade-off between reconstruction quality and semantic fidelity, highlighting the effectiveness of AFs fusion architecture. Block-wise MoT. To evaluate the effectiveness of Block-wise MoT, we compare it with an MMDiT-based flow head architecture (Xie et al., 2025) under the same AF tokenizer, DDT-based predictor, and text-to-image pretraining settings. As shown in Fig. 9, Block-wise MoT achieves higher GenEval scores than MMDiT throughout training, despite using fewer generation-specific parameters (891M vs. 962M). These results suggest that Block-wise MoT effectively leverages pretrained VLM representations for visual generation with smaller additional capacity.

sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: Unified multimodal models. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) aim to integrate visual understanding and generation within single framework. Early approaches pursued native unification by representing different modalities as discrete tokens and modeling them with common autoregressive objective (Lu et al., 2024; Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Recent work has increasingly incorporated continuous visual representations with diffusionor flow-based generation objectives alongside autoregressive language modeling (Zhou et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025). To accommodate the resulting heterogeneity between understanding and generation, several approaches introduce taskor modalityspecific pathways while retaining varying degrees of shared computation. For example, Janus decouples the visual encoding pathways for understanding and generation (Wu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b), while some approaches introduce specialized transformer experts while retaining shared cross-modal interaction (Liang et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025). Other approaches couple pretrained visual language models with dedicated generative pathways (Pan et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2025b; Pan et al., 2026), but these approaches rely on separate generative representations. In contrast, Integral constructs shared visual representation aligned with the pretrained VLMs native features, enabling its existing multimodal knowledge to contribute to image generation. Visual representations for understanding and generation. Visual understanding and generation have traditionally relied on different types of visual representations. Semantic encoders learn transferable, high-level visual features, whereas generative tokenizers are primarily trained to retain information needed for image reconstruction (Radford et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2023; Esser et al., 2021). Recent work has explored pretrained semantic representations for generation (Zheng et al., 2026; Singh et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b), as well as visual tokenizers that combine or separate semantic and reconstructive information (Ma et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a; Yang 10 et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026). These approaches often address the trade-off between semantic preservation and reconstruction quality (Ma et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026). In contrast, Integral constructs shared visual representation aligned with the pretrained VLMs native features, enabling its multimodal knowledge to support visual generation.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Integral, unified multimodal model that extends pretrained vision-language model with strong visual generation while preserving multimodal understanding. Despite using only 0.89B generation-specific parameters, Integral achieves strong performance across compositional generation, knowledge-intensive generation, and multimodal image editing. Our results show that sharing the visual representation space between understanding and generation is key to transferring multimodal knowledge to visual generation.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: A.1 Architecture Abstraction Fusion. We use the vision encoder of Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026), consisting of 27 transformer blocks with patch size 16 and hidden dimension dh = 1152. AF aggregates all 28 representations, including the patch embeddings and the outputs of each transformer block. Each representation is normalized using fixed per-layer statistics computed from 50K ImageNet training images. To enable efficient self-attention across encoder layers, we jointly project every four consecutive layers into single feature, resulting in seven layer-wise features per spatial position. These features are then aggregated using self-attention layer with 16 heads, followed by linear pooler that produces fused representations of dimension df = 1152. Variational bottleneck and decoders. The fused representations are compressed into 256-dimensional latent space through variational bottleneck, which predicts the mean and log-variance of diagonal Gaussian distribution. We sample from this distribution during training and use the posterior mean at inference. For image reconstruction, we adopt the ViT-XL decoder from RAE (Zheng et al., 2026), consisting of 28 transformer layers with width 1152. The semantic projector merges each 2 2 neighborhood of visual tokens and projects them to the pretrained VLMs visual input dimension ds = 4096. Block-wise MoT. We attach eight generation blocks to the 32-layer language backbone of Qwen3.5-9B at intervals of four layers. To reduce generation-specific parameters, we match the attention QKV dimensions to those of the pretrained VLM while using reduced hidden dimension of dg = 2048 for the remaining computations. The generative stream is initialized through two-layer MLP. Each generation block uses queries from the generative stream and keys and values from both the generative stream and the corresponding frozen VLM layer. We apply timestep conditioning through adaLN-single (Chen et al., 2023) and use DDT-based prediction head (Wang et al., 2026a) with two transformer blocks of width 3072. The noisy visual latents are processed only by the generative pathway, leaving the pretrained VLM unchanged. A.2 Training We train Integral in two phases: visual tokenizer training and generation training. Each phase consists of three stages, as summarized in Tab. 7. Visual tokenization. We first train AF at 256256 resolution, followed by dynamic-resolution training up to 512512. The tokenizer is optimized with reconstruction, semantic alignment, and KL regularization losses. The reconstruction loss combines pixel-wise ℓ1 and LPIPS losses, while the semantic alignment loss is implemented as Lsem = 1 1 + (cid:2)MSE(ˆs, s) + MSE(cid:0)ˆs, s(cid:1)(cid:3) , (6) where denotes per-token RMS normalization. We set = 0.3, λsem = 5.0, and βKL = 106. In the final tokenizer stage, we fine-tune only the pixel decoder with adversarial supervision while keeping the learned visual latent space fixed. Following RAE (Zheng et al., 2026), we use discriminator based on frozen DINO ViT-S/8 with trainable heads and optimize the hinge adversarial objective. The adversarial loss is enabled after 5K steps with weight of 0.5, scaled by an adaptive weight following VQGAN (Esser et al., 2021). Visual generation. We use the posterior mean of the trained AF tokenizer as the generation target, standardized using per-channel statistics computed from 50K ImageNet training images. For flow matching, we adopt logit-normal timestep sampling with time shift of 4.0 (Esser et al., 2024). Visual generation training consists of three stages. We first perform text-to-image pretraining at 256 256 resolution. We then conduct interleaved pretraining at resolutions up to 512 512 to support multimodal conditional generation. Finally, interleaved supervised fine-tuning (SFT) covers text-to-image generation, image editing, multi-reference generation, and interleaved reasoning. Datasets. For visual tokenizer training, we use DataComp-1B (Gadre et al., 2023) for the initial training and additionally incorporate BLIP-3o (Chen et al., 2025a) and RenderedText (Wendler, 2024) for dynamic-resolution training. The adversarial decoder training uses DataComp-1B. 18 For visual generation training, text-to-image pretraining uses BLIP-3o, RenderedText, and TextAtlas5M (Wang et al., 2025a). Interleaved pretraining additionally incorporates ScaleEdit-12M (Chen et al., 2026), TextSculpt-Data (Lin et al., 2026), Pico-Banana-400K, and image reconstruction data from ImageNet-1K (Russakovsky et al., 2015) and BLIP-3o. For interleaved SFT, we use GPT-Image-Edit-1.5M (Wang et al., 2025b), Echo-4o-Image (Ye et al., 2025a), OpenGPT-4o-Image (Chen et al., 2025c), ScaleEdit-12M, Nano-Consistent-150K, TextSculpt-Data, Zebra-CoT (Li et al., 2026), and image reconstruction data. sections.title: C Additional Ablation Studies
sections.content: We provide additional analyses of AF and Block-wise MoT, including component ablations, the contributions of encoder layers, and computational efficiency. C.1 Abstraction Fusion Component ablations. We examine the contributions of individual components in AF under matched 20K-step tokenizer training settings. As shown in Tab. 10, replacing per-layer normalization and projection with shared counterparts or removing self-attention degrades reconstruction quality and semantic similarity. Replacing self-attention and linear pooling with attention pooling further reduces both metrics, supporting the effectiveness of the proposed fusion architecture. Semantic supervision. We compare AF with AF w/o sem., which removes the semantic alignment objective while keeping the tokenizer architecture and other training settings unchanged. As shown in Tab. 11 and Fig. 10, AF w/o sem. achieves higher reconstruction fidelity (33.7 vs. 32.2 dB PSNR) but substantially lower generation performance across GenEval, WISE-Verified, and DPG-Bench. These results further support the importance of semantic supervision for generative learning. Contributions of encoder layers. To examine how AF utilizes hierarchical visual features, we analyze the learned attention distribution across encoder layers and progressively remove features from different depths. As shown in (a) GenEval (b) DPG-Bench (c) WISE-Verified Figure 10 Effect of semantic supervision. Generation performance during 50K-step text-to-image training with and without semantic alignment. (a) Cross-layer attention (b) Removing the deepest layers (c) Removing the shallowest layers Figure 11 Contribution of features across encoder depth. (a) Average cross-layer attention across layer groups. (b) Reconstruction quality when removing the deepest layers. (c) Semantic similarity when removing the shallowest layers. Fig. 11a, AF distributes attention across the encoder hierarchy, including shallow, intermediate, and deep layers. Figs. 11b and 11c further show that removing deeper-layer features reduces reconstruction quality, while removing shallower-layer features degrades semantic similarity. These results indicate that features across different encoder depths contribute to the learned representation. C.2 Block-wise MoT We further compare Block-wise MoT with Full MoT, which attaches generation block to each of the 31 VLM layers. Both variants use the same AF tokenizer and 50K-step text-to-image pretraining settings. As shown in Tab. 13, Block-wise MoT achieves comparable generation performance to Full MoT across GenEval, WISE-Verified, and DPGBench while using substantially fewer generation blocks. These results support the use of sparse interactions with the pretrained VLM for visual generation. C.3 Computational Efficiency We evaluate the computational overhead of AF for multimodal understanding and the inference efficiency of Blockwise MoT for visual generation. Overhead of AF. The AF module and semantic projector replace the original visual processing pathway, increasing its parameter count from 456.0M to 582.1M (+126.1M). The pixel decoder contains an additional 475.1M parameters and is used for image reconstruction. We measure inference latency and peak GPU memory using single 800 800 image and 100 generated text tokens. As shown in Tab. 12, AF introduces modest overhead in end-to-end understanding inference, increasing latency by 2.1% and peak memory by 7.3%. Efficiency of Block-wise MoT.
